title: Shoftim: justice, justice (Deuteronomy 16:20)
hookLine: "Justice, justice shalt thou follow"; the doubled word means just ends by just means

lines: ON A POSTER, A WALL, A SIGN.
cards: It turns up on posters, on courthouse walls, on protest signs. Two words, repeated: justice, justice. In a language where one word is usually enough, the Torah says this one twice, and close readers have asked why.
The Talmud asks. Centuries later, the Hasidic teachers ask again. The answers don't cancel each other out.
They stack, like layers, each one turning the doubled word a little and catching a different light.

teach.b: In the old Jewish translation: "Justice, justice shalt thou follow, that thou mayest live, and inherit the land which the LORD thy God giveth thee." In Hebrew, tzedek tzedek tirdof.
Tzedek is today's word: justice, rightness. It's the root of tzedakah, from a few days ago.
And tirdof doesn't really mean follow. It means pursue, chase, run after. Justice isn't something you wait for.
Now the double. The Talmud, in Sanhedrin, offers a few readings.
One: the first justice is strict law, the second is compromise. A court should know when to rule, and when to help two sides settle. Another: pursue a good court; travel to the wisest judges.
And a reading that became well-known much later, often attributed to the Hasidic teacher Rabbi Simcha Bunim of Peshischa: pursue justice justly.
You can't chase justice by cheating, by lying, by trampling people on the way. The road has to be as just as the place you're trying to reach.

The verse right before gives a sharp example: a judge must not take a gift, because a gift blinds the eyes of the wise. A bribe doesn't just tempt; it changes what you can see. So the doubled word guards both ends.
The goal must be just, and so must the road.

how: Tzedek tzedek tirdof is often quoted in Jewish life, inscribed in some synagogues and courthouses and cited by Jewish organizations working for social and legal justice.

o: justice, rightness, a thing to pursue
charity, money given to the poor
a judge who sits at the town gate

games.q: inside the doubled word — tap the pairs.
p: blinds the eyes of the wise

s: tirdof means to follow quietly behind
it means pursue, chase, run after.
the Talmud reads the doubled justice as law and compromise
tzedek shares a root with tzedakah

games.q: you're sure your cause is just, and bending the truth a little would help you win. what does the reading attributed to Rabbi Bunim say?
o: a just goal excuses the means.
pursue justice justly: just ends by just means.
games.why: the doubled tzedek guards both ends: the goal and the road there must both be just.

practice: Think of something you're in the right about, a dispute with a sibling, a cause you care about, an argument at work, and look only at the means.
Have you pursued it with accurate words or exaggerations, with respect for the other side or contempt, with patience or pressure? Find the one place where the road has been less just than the goal.

wordCard.voice: Tzedek. Justice, rightness. Said twice in Shoftim, and pursued, not waited for.

orig.note: Hebrew: justice, rightness. said twice in Deuteronomy 16:20, the root of tzedakah.

carryVoice: Your line: justice, justice. The goal and the road there both have to count. See you tomorrow.
